result: Early stages of scale cell development in papilionid butterflies (P. eurimedes and P. polytes) follow the same pattern as previously documented in nymphalid species, with F-actin bundles forming and laying down a scaffold that determines ridge position. This extends previous observations to Papilionidae and supports the hypothesis that this mechanism is broadly conserved across lepidopterans.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly accept this finding. Reviewer 1 states 'the article shows good microscopy data, including detailed, dense developmental series' and Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'extended previous observations that parallel F-actin bundles configure the spacing and position of longitudinal ridges.' The editor describes the work as 'convincingly show[ing]' the findings. No concerns are raised about these early developmental observations.

result: At 48-52% development in P. eurimedes, irregular crossrib patterns appear in the plasma membrane between ridges, serving as a template for chitin accretion into cuticular disks. This marks the beginning of honeycomb lattice formation and represents a novel finding about papilionid scale development.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this as a novel finding. Reviewer 1 describes the data as 'interesting and novel' and notes 'the mix of cell membrane staining, chitin precursor, and F-actin staining is well utilized.' The editor emphasizes the work 'convincingly show[s]' the findings using 'state-of-the-art microscopy techniques.' No concerns are raised about these observations of crossrib pattern formation.

result: F-actin bundles in P. eurimedes undergo a novel reorganization process after ridge formation (57-76% development), breaking down and reorganizing into a reticulate network surrounding cuticular disks. This reorganized actin network likely draws the plasma membrane and overlying cuticle inward, molding it into the honeycomb lattice walls. This represents a previously unconsidered role for F-actin in papilionid scale morphogenesis.
evaluation: Reviewers strongly support this as the key novel finding. Reviewer 1 states 'The key message from this article is that F-actin filaments are later repurposed, in papilionid butterflies, to finish the patterning of the inter-ridge space, elaborating new structures (this was not observed so far in other studies and organisms).' The editor describes the work as showing 'F-actin is utilized in these butterflies in a novel way to produce structure.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'the intricate f-actin filaments reorganise, support cuticular discs that template the air holes that form the honeycomb lattice.'

result: Arp2/3 complex shows temporal association with F-actin reorganization in P. eurimedes, with punctate patterns appearing during actin disintegration and reorganization (52-62% development). CK-666 inhibition experiments show some effect on honeycomb lattice height when applied at 52% development, with time-dependent effects suggesting a developmental window for Arp2/3 involvement.
evaluation: Reviewers express caution about these findings. Reviewer 1 notes 'The authors performed immunolocalizations of Arp2 and pharmacological inhibitions of Arp2/3, and found some possible effect on honeycomb lattice development... These data provide circumstantial evidence that Arp2/3 is involved.' The use of 'possible effect' and 'circumstantial evidence' indicates uncertainty. Reviewer 2 mentions the work is 'based on a somewhat limited sample size for their focus species, limiting attempts to suppress expression and alter structure shape,' suggesting the inhibition experiments are not fully conclusive.

result: P. polytes, which has irregular crossribs without deep honeycomb lattice walls, shows neither cuticular disk formation nor F-actin reorganization during development. Arp2/3 inhibition does not affect ridge or crossrib formation in this species. This suggests that cuticular disk formation and F-actin reorganization are restricted to species with elaborate honeycomb lattice walls.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this comparative finding. Reviewer 1 notes 'The inter-ridge region of the butterfly Papilio polytes, which lacks these structures, did not seem to be affected by drug treatments. Effects were time-dependent, which makes sense.' This comparative data strengthens the main findings by showing species-specificity. No concerns are raised about these observations.

result: Comparative observations across additional papilionid species (P. arcas, P. nireus, P. palinurus) show variations in F-actin reorganization patterns that correspond to different honeycomb and dimpled scale morphologies. In P. palinurus, F-actin reorganizes into concave networks corresponding to cuticular dimples, suggesting an extreme modification of the honeycomb developmental program.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these comparative findings but note limitations. Reviewer 1 states 'The authors perform a comparative study in additional papilionids (Fig. 6 in particular). I find these data to be quite limited without a dense sampling, but they are nonetheless interesting and support a second-phase role of F-actin re-organisation.' The findings are accepted as supporting evidence despite limited sampling, indicating they strengthen the main conclusions about F-actin's role.
